data.title: Nepal's catastrophic flooding is a red alert for the world's mountain towns
data.description:
In 2011, I trekked with scientists and engineers to about 17,000 feet to look at Lake Imja in Nepal’s Everest region. I thought about that expedition from the safety of my home in Peru as I watched the awful consequences of permafrost weakened by warming upon the northern district of Rasuwa, near Nepal’s border with Tibet. 

When glaciers recede, they leave an indent created by their weight. Melt from the glacier fills that bowl, growing until the pressure gets too great, or an earthquake hits. Lake Imja did not exist in 1953, when Sir Edmund Hillary conquered Everest. By 2011, it was the fastest-growing of some 1,600 glacier lakes in Nepal.

On our visit, the artificial lake stretched down from the glacier for a mile and a half, held in place by a precarious mix of debris. An earthquake or pressure on the makeshift dam could release water with disastrous consequences for vulnerable communities in Nepal. 

On Aug. 26, the world watched the consequences of a different version of what we feared. Above Rasuwa, a broken chunk of glacier, likely the size of a big New York City building, fell 4,000 feet, setting off a tsunami. Friction at that velocity melts ice. A great wave gathered ice, snow, water, rocks and mud — and then structures — to cascade down the narrow valleys, wiping out lives, communities and infrastructure. Hurricane-force winds leveled trees. 

I’m safe as I write, but some version of the same can and likely will happen in my country and other mountainous regions, and again in Nepal. Towers of ice and snow weakened by a quickly heating planet will, one way or another, wreak havoc down-mountain in vulnerable landscapes.  

We came back from our Lake Imja expedition shaken, but also with thoughts about how to anticipate and prepare against these disasters.  

Early warning systems with real-time sensors and satellite communications can detect sudden water releases and alert downstream communities. It could help to slowly lower water levels in high-risk glacial lakes and, where possible, to future-proofing buildings and installations. Lake Imja was a slightly different situation than what happened in Rasuwa, but it carries the same danger and is more like the situation in my country.  

In Peru, Palcacocha is a glacial lake in Huaraz Province. The spectacular snow-covered peaks of that part of the Andes mountain range are warming, creating the same conditions as we saw in Nepal. One hundred thousand people live below our lake, including communities and schools that inevitably will be directly in the pathway should meltwater be released and trigger a chain reaction not unlike what happened in Nepal.   

Part of my job as executive director of the Instituto Andino de Montaña in Peru was to persuade the city of Huaraz to put an early warning system in place. After much effort, we achieved that. But when we tried to get officials to commit to engineering to lower the lake’s water level, we encountered red tape, indolence, wrong priorities and fear of scaring away tourists. No funding or commitment was forthcoming.   

Since then, we have been holding our breath and hoping for the best. But with the ongoing El Niño event, this could be the season when our worst fears come about.   

The grassroots Peruvians I work with in the countryside have no trust that government officials will protect them against these well-known risks. Huaraz is very far from Lima, our capital, and the people at risk feel invisible. Officials at the federal level are trying to pass the buck to local and private actors. But no one at the local, provincial or even regional level has the technical capacity to take on this challenging engineering work.  

The U.S., where I got my Ph.D., is not immune. Melting glaciers already trigger disastrous floods and mudslides. A glacial lake outburst flood has occurred every year since 2011 at Suicide Basin, on the Mendenhall Glacier near Juneau, Alaska. The rapid retreat of the Grasshopper Glacier in Wyoming’s Wind River Mountains triggered a glacial lake outburst flood in 2003.

American communities will suffer a quieter, less visible threat — the toxic minerals and metals from melting glaciers that leak into local water supplies, eroding life rather than blasting it away.

If disaster happens anywhere, in my country, or any number of American communities as this threat evolves, there will be official mourning. Why not invest that energy and empathy into acting now and saving lives, rather than grieving them?

Jorge Recharte Bullard Ph.D. has served as president of Instituto Andino de Montaña, the Mountain Institute’s Legacy Institution, since 2020. He was director of the Andean program of The Mountain Institute between 1997 and 2019.

data.title: Trump posts GOP senator's cell phone number over daylight savings act stall
data.description:
President Trump posted Sen. Tom Cotton’s (R-Ark.) cell phone number on Truth Social Saturday, lashing out at Senate Republicans to move forward with legislation that would make daylight saving time permanent.

“Tom Cotton, a friend of mine, is holding up a very important Bill,” Trump wrote, describing the Sunshine Protection Act. “For some reason, Tom is stopping the Bill and, in the Senate, it’s very easy to do, it only takes one! It should pass overwhelmingly, in a Bipartisan fashion.”

“To the Great People of Arkansas, please let your Senator know it would be a GREAT Bipartisan WIN for the United States Senate, and for America, itself. Call Tom on his cellphone,” the president continued before he wrote the number. “Let him know.”

Trump blamed Cotton for the bill — which he called the “No More Changing of Clocks Act” — stalling in the Senate after it passed the House with a 308-117 vote.

Cotton has been among the most vocal opponents of permanent daylight saving time —expressing concern that without the twice a year clock changes, many children heading to school and millions of Americans traveling to work would be left in the dark.

“If permanent daylight saving time becomes the law of the land, it will again make winter a dark and dismal time for millions of Americans,” he said last year.

Trump countered that more evening daylight would help reduce crime and traffic accidents, while benefiting public health and industries including sports, tourism, restaurants and retail.

In his Saturday Truth Social post, Trump continued that the bill would help the PGA Tour who “needs more Daylight in the afternoon in order to finish their Tournaments.”

“Likewise, regular Golfers, Tennis Players, Hunters and, perhaps most importantly, Farmers who want more Daylight to play or work,” he added.

The post included a letter from PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp who wrote in “strong support” of the bill — citing that it would generate $1 billion annually in new direct revenue for the sport. 

Trump has pushed for the Sunshine Protect Act’s passage since August, but Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) has cast doubt on whether the measure can secure the 60 votes needed to advance.

Cotton’s office did not respond immediately to The Hill’s request for comment.

data.title: Pennsylvania nears 1,000 measles cases, state health department reports
data.description:
Pennsylvania’s reported measles cases are almost at 1,000 for 2026, days after its health department confirmed the figure had passed 900.

“977 measles cases have been confirmed across 39 counties in Pennsylvania so far in 2026,” Pennsylvania’s Department of Health wrote in a statement Friday. 

The agency highlighted that 34 new Pennsylvania measles cases had emerged since Sept. 30, with hospitalizations tied to the infection reaching 195. The statement also reemphasized the state’s reported five measles-associated deaths amid an ongoing dispute between Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. over the outbreak’s true death toll.

The outbreak is the worst the commonwealth has seen in more than 35 years.

Pennsylvania’s Department of Health added Friday that all but four of its measles cases have been among people who were not fully vaccinated against the virus.

“In a typical month, Pennsylvania health care providers administer approximately 25,000 doses of the MMR vaccine,” it wrote. “In August 2026, more than 49,000 MMR vaccines were administered and so far in September 2026, more than 53,000 doses have been administered.”

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) describes measles as a highly contagious virus but adds that two doses of the MMR vaccine provide the best protection. Pennsylvania’s health department stated that both doses together are 97 percent effective at preventing measles for life.

Earlier this month, the Pennsylvania Department of Health began the process of requesting emergency assistance from the CDC’s Epi-Aid program following five reported deaths tied to the infection, but only on the condition that the federal agency publicly recognizes the state’s entire reported death count. 

The CDC has refused to acknowledge the same number of deaths as the Keystone State in its national count, sparking a bitter political dispute between Shapiro and Kennedy over what constitutes a measles death.  

The federal agency to date has only recognized two deaths in its measles cases and outbreaks index, though the website adds that “this number is subject to change.”

The CDC’s database does not specify where or when these deaths occurred, so it’s not clear if the tally includes Pennsylvania’s reported cases. However, no other state has recorded a measles death this year. 

In 2025, three people in the U.S. died from measles — two in Texas and one in New Mexico.

data.title: Check your email: Notices sent regarding $309M Amazon returns settlement
data.description:
(NEXSTAR) – If you’ve returned an item you bought via Amazon over a several-year period, you may qualify for payment in a new class action settlement.

Back in January, the online retail giant agreed to pay $309 million to settle claims that customers were wrongly denied refunds for product returns. Reuters reported that Amazon, while denying any wrongdoing, will also provide other benefits as part of the settlement.

In a statement to the outlet, an Amazon spokesperson said an internal review in 2025 uncovered “a small subset of returns where we issued a refund without the payment completing, or where we could not verify that the correct item had been sent back to us, so no refund had been issued.”

Settlement administrators announced last week that while a proposed settlement has been agreed upon, it awaits court approval. The court has also not found Amazon “liable in any way,” or that the company “engaged in any wrongdoing or misconduct of any kind.”

Some have started to receive notices (which may be in your email’s spam folder) that they qualify for payment, according to posts on Reddit.

Who qualifies for payment?

First, you need to have started a return to Amazon or asked for a refund for a product purchased on Amazon and received in the U.S. between Sept. 5, 2017, and Feb. 12, 2026. Further, you need to have either not received a refund, even though you should have, or your refund from Amazon was “untimely or incorrect,” and/or, you received a refund only to later be charged by Amazon, incorrectly, for the product or products that you were returning.

Settlement administrators explain that Amazon implemented a process to pay refunds to the customers it found were impacted as part of the aforementioned 2025 internal review. Those payments are separate from the settlement’s common fund, which Amazon is paying $309.5 million into.

After paying other costs and expenses associated with the settlement, the fund will be divided among two subclasses of class members. Members of both are “expected to receive a full refund plus interest,” but they vary in how much proof they need to provide that they qualify.

Subclass A, which will receive more than 92% of the remaining funds, according to the settlement administrators, qualify for automatic payments. These customers were impacted by “computer and payment processing errors,” court documents explained, or Amazon records showed the return wasn’t completed, “for example, because said return was potentially lost in transit.” These members will not have to file a claim but will need to identify their preferred payment option after the court approves the settlement.

Subclass B, meanwhile, will need to submit claims that show “more likely than not” that they are entitled to payment, per court documents. These customers need also to have “experienced failed refunds or retrocharges,” but Amazon’s available records “do not establish that it is more likely than not Amazon incorrectly processed the return.”

You may fall into both subclasses, but your payouts may arrive as a single payment, administrators said.

How to submit a claim

If you qualify for the settlement, you can expect to receive notification via email of your status. This will include a Notice ID and Confirmation Code that you will use to file a claim online, if you are a member of Subclass B. Paper forms are also available, but you will need to mail them in.

The form asks you to provide your contact information as well as details about the returns that were rejected or the incorrect refunds you received through Amazon. You will also need to identify your preferred payout option.

Should your claim be verified, the available options include an Amazon gift card, a check, PayPal, Venmo, Zelle, and a virtual prepaid card.

You’ll have until Dec. 1, 2026, to submit your claim.

What else should I know about this proposed settlement?

You can find more details about the settlement here.

It is still pending court approval, with a hearing scheduled for March 16, 2027. That date could move, and any appeals of the decision could delay the payout process.

Should the settlement be approved, Subclass A members will have 105 days to select their preferred payout option.

data.title: The Trump administration needs a crash course in 'Working Class' from JD Vance
data.description:
Note to Republican leadership: If you truly deem the Democrats coming back into power in Congress and the White House as an existential threat to our nation, then why are you handing them the winning issue for this election cycle on a silver platter? 

To be sure, there are still millions of Americans who believe President Trump has an exceptional understanding of economics and that the “business of America is business.” That said, they also understand that Trump is a leader who was blessed to grow up in a bubble of wealth and privilege. 

As such, the day-to-day struggles of working-class Americans, no matter how much Trump may sympathize, are still only academic to him.  

Our 45th and 47th president has never experienced the hope-crushing and mentally debilitating realities millions of Americans face each waking morning. Realities such as: not having enough money to pay the rent or mortgage; the threat of eviction; being forced to choose between heating fuel or food; not having enough money to buy your child needed medicine; having to walk to your minimum wage job because you did not have enough money to buy gas for your car; not having the money to move from your crime-infested neighborhood; not having the money to fix your teeth; or not having the money so your child could attend the prom. 

I can assure you, as someone who grew up in abject poverty and was homeless as a child, millions of our fellow Americans are dealing with these issues every single day. Just as I can assure you that having people in bubbles of wealth and privilege tell paycheck-to-paycheck working Americans to “suck it up” so we can prevent Iran from getting a nuclear weapon is infuriating. 

I have spoken with many Republicans and Trump supporters who have continually asked over the last few months: “Wait a minute, I thought the president said we obliterated Iran’s nuclear capability last year! So why am I now being forced to pay higher gas prices and tell my family we can no longer afford meat?” 

No matter if the Republican leadership wants to admit it or not, they have a growing perception problem with working-class and disenfranchised Americans. These voters not only believe the Republicans have greatly exacerbated their daily financial struggles but are simultaneously telling them to stop whining for the good of the nation. It’s not a winning strategy in the voting booth. 

Working-class Americans don’t need lectures from privileged politicians, pundits and academics. They need a champion, preferably one who lived in and escaped their world into a position of leadership, where they can actually do something about it.  

Fortunately for Trump and the Republican leadership, literally right down the hall from the Oval Office sits a man who has a veritable Ph.D. in “working class American.” That person is Vice President JD Vance.   

If there is one person in the Trump administration whose life story can deeply resonate with the working class of our nation, it is Vance’s. As he described in his best-selling novel “Hillbilly Elegy,” our vice president grew up a child of divorce in the Rust Belt, as his mother struggled against addiction and alcohol abuse. Vance served in the Marines and put himself through college and law school. He rose quickly in politics, from the Senate to the White House —a life story that speaks to virtually every demographic in one way or another.   

In our increasingly polarized and siloed country, many Americans may have forgotten or never learned of Vance’s remarkable story. Now might be a good time for Vance to not only remind voters that he is “one of them,” but the Republican leadership as well. 

Years ago, I had the honor to work in the White House for two presidents. If memory serves, there is a very nice auditorium in the Eisenhower Executive Office Building where the privileged leadership of the Trump administration can be gathered so the vice president can give them a crash course in the increasingly harsh realities faced by the working class of our nation on a daily basis. 

Let’s not lecture the working class, Vance should emphasize. Let’s not speak down to them. Let’s not blame them or insult them. Rather, let us listen to them, empathize with them and seek to help them. 

If the Republicans want to have any hope of not being drowned by a growing blue wave come Nov. 3, they would do tell to listen and learn. 

Douglas MacKinnon is a former White House and Pentagon official.

data.title: Pike's botched execution renews death penalty scrutiny
data.description:
Tennessee’s botched execution of Christa Pike is renewing scrutiny over how states carry out the death penalty and raising questions about what legal recourse exists when that protocol goes awry.   

The attempt mirrors recent failures in other states, where inmates and their lawyers have argued in court that such errors amount to cruel and unusual punishment under the Eighth Amendment.  

“What happened here gives attorneys and courts both within and outside of Tennessee a new factual example that they’re certainly going to consider when evaluating any reliability of these procedures and any implications under the Eighth Amendment,” said Paul Lucas, an associate professor of criminal justice at East Carolina University in Greenville, N.C.   

Pike, 50, was sentenced to death a year after confessing to the brutal 1995 torture and murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a Jobs Corps classmate, at an abandoned steam plant in Knoxville. 

Pike was set to be executed by lethal injection Wednesday morning, but it was delayed for hours following a last-minute stay by the 6th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. That was ultimately lifted by the U.S. Supreme Court over the dissent of the three liberal justices.   

The state’s attempt to execute her that night went disastrously. Witnesses in the death chamber reported Pike was still alive and snoring after being administered two syringes of the lethal injection drug pentobarbital.   

Pike’s case is one of many within the past decade in which executioners either struggled to find a vein or the drugs didn’t work as expected, leading inmates to need additional doses or endure minutes of severe pain before the effects took hold.   

“I think there’s been an assumption that pentobarbital protocols comply with the Constitution,” said Bo King, a capital postconviction attorney based in North Carolina who’s represented dozens of clients on death row and witnessed five executions.   

“That is being challenged by botches like we saw with Ms. Pike,” he said, also pointing to another Tennessee case from last year in which an inmate complained that it was “hurting so bad” minutes after being injected with the drug.

Fourteen states and the federal government currently use a single-drug lethal injection protocol that most commonly relies on an overdose of pentobarbital, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. The barbiturate acts as a sedative that, when taken in high enough doses, can suppress the nervous system to the point of coma, cardiovascular collapse and death.

But it’s not always effective. The Biden administration stopped using the drug after a Justice Department review noted concerns that it may cause “unnecessary pain and suffering.” President Trump reversed that decision when he returned to office, reauthorizing its use in federal executions.   

Pike was taken to the hospital about two hours after doses were administered. The state that had just failed to execute her was now responsible for facilitating life-saving care. She remained in critical condition as of Friday, according to her lawyers. 

The state’s governor, Republican Bill Lee, has paused executions through the end of the year and ordered an independent, third-party review of what happened. 

“Carrying out a lawfully imposed sentence is among the State’s most serious responsibilities, and the people of Tennessee expect it to be done in a manner that is not only legal and constitutional, but is effective,” the governor said in a statement.   

Pike’s lawyers want any further attempts to execute her off the table for good.   

“After having endured solitary confinement for more than 20 years and a full attempt to kill her by lethal injection, Christa has endured punishment greater than any other person in the history of the American death penalty,” attorney Randy Spivey said during a press conference. “The governor must commute Christa’s sentence now.”  

Their reprieve argument hinges on the idea that while the Constitution does not guarantee a painless execution, it does forbid “superadded” pain or terror in carrying out a death sentence. That standard has been repeatedly upheld and used by the Supreme Court to evaluate various challenges to state execution methods in the modern era. 

In the landmark 2008 case of Baze v. Rees, the majority found that an execution method is only unconstitutional if it presents a “substantial” or “objectively intolerable” risk of serious harm and there is a feasible, readily available alternative that would significantly reduce that risk.    

The high court adopted similar logic in rejecting challenges to Oklahoma’s and Missouri’s lethal injection protocols in 2015 and 2018, respectively.   

Because the bar to prove cruel and unusual punishment is so high, legal experts say that challenges often turn on the specifics of how an execution is carried out.   

Lucas suggested that is why the outcome of the review in Pike’s case will be critical in determining whether the state may ultimately try again.  

“The question would be whether, knowing what Tennessee knows now from its first attempt, subjecting Ms. Pike to another execution, is it going to be under the same or similar procedures?” Lucas said. “That is what creates the unconstitutional risk of severe pain.”   

Attorneys also face another complication when litigating postconviction claims in court: The capital punishment process in most states is shrouded in secrecy. 

“The secrecy statutes conceal the information about the drugs themselves, or the protocols … that the state wants to use in an execution,” King explained. “It’s difficult to assess whether there’s a constitutional problem, much less bring a constitutional challenge, without that very basic information about how the state proposes to execute your client.” 

Still, the “superadded pain” defense has been successful before, at least temporarily.  

In June, the Supreme Court blocked Alabama from executing convicted murderer Jeffery Lee by nitrogen gas after an appeals court found the method unconstitutionally cruel. The state ultimately moved forward with a different method, lethal injection, and put Lee to death last month.   

Pike, the only woman on Tennessee’s death row, is not alone when it comes to botched executions. Tennessee also botched the execution of Tony Carruthers in May, and the Death Penalty Information Center estimates there have been at least 64 instances of botched executions across the U.S. since 1982.  

Although the electric chair remains an available method in a handful of states, it has not been used since 2020. 

“Every major method of execution has had at least one botch since 2025,” King said. 

The rate is highest among lethal injections, and experts note that litigating those cases is difficult because courts don’t generally view isolated mishaps as standalone grounds for permanent reprieve from the death penalty.  

Pike is believed to be the first person in modern history to have survived an execution attempt once the drugs were already administered, and that has put the issue in uncharted territory. 

“With this real-world data point, we’re going to see more litigation coming through the courts, and the outcome of that, with what happened with Ms. Pike and, of course, Tennessee, will inform that,” he later added.

Lucas also noted that the uptick in lethal injection-related litigation coupled with difficulty obtaining the lethal drugs has pushed states to search for alternative methods. 

Five states — Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah — have authorized the use of a firing squad. South Carolina executed three men via that method last year, the only state to do so since 2010.   

King represented all three of those men. Lawyers claimed a botched execution in one of those cases, arguing that Mikal Mahdi endured some suffering after the bullets that were intended to kill him immediately largely missed his heart. The state disputes that claim.   

Those failures, he said, point to larger systemic issues that leave families on both sides hanging in the balance.   

“A botched execution or protracted execution does nothing to ease the suffering of anyone involved,” King said. “It leaves everyone in this limbo of uncertainty and pain, and I have a hard time understanding how anyone is served by that.”

data.title: Man arrested for alleged terror threat on US airbase RAF Fairford released on bail
data.description:
The U.K.-Iranian dual national who was arrested in connection with an alleged terror threat against a U.S.-operated military base in England was released on bail, British authorities confirmed Saturday.

The 25-year-old man was taken into custody in the City of Westminster, London, earlier this week on “suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts” targeting RAF Fairford — a British-owned American air base.

A local farmer was the first to report the incident to law enforcement, telling police there were three suspicious vehicles and a group of men wearing masks near the base late at night on Sept. 26. The U.S. Air Force has used the military facility to position B-52 and B-1 bombers as part of the Trump administration’s war in Iran.

“Searches of two properties in the same area have now concluded,” British Counterterrorism Police wrote. “The investigation into the circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is continuing.”

In a separate update, Senior National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing Vicki Evans said, “The investigation into circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of enquiry.”

“As we’ve made clear, we’re looking at all possible angles – including possible foreign state involvement. I’d like to thank the public for their continued support and patience whilst we work through this investigation.”

The other five men involved in the incident were U.K. nationals in their 20s. British Counterterrorism Police confirmed on Oct. 1 that all of these men remain on police bail.

U.K. authorities have not released the names of any of the men arrested in connection with the suspected terror plot.

When asked on Monday about the other five men’s bail, President Trump told reporters in the Oval Office he was “surprised that they released them.”

“I would’ve said don’t let them have bail,” the president added.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Wednesday his government believes that Iran “played a part” in the incident. Trump also said he suspects the Islamic Republic “might be” involved.

The Iranian Embassy in London said in a Monday statement that it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran to arrest of five suspects in the vicinity of RAF Fairford base.”

data.title: Trump thanks man who helped save Flydubai flight: 'What a job he did, he's a hero'
data.description:
President Trump on Friday morning thanked the Israeli plumber, Yaniv Hayoun, who intervened after a pilot stabbed his co-pilot and attempted to crash a Flydubai flight this week. 

In a video message shared on Truth Social, the president praised Hayoun, saying he “did an amazing job.”

“He’s my kind of guy,” he continued. “He can be my plumber. He can be whatever he wants to be. What a job he did. He’s a hero, and I want to just congratulate him and his family.”

Hayoun worked with three other passengers to subdue the pilot before he took control of the jet’s steering controls to stabilize the aircraft, which had descended into free fall during the attack. 

The plumber, who had no formal flight training, said he relied on his knowledge from watching “Air Crash Investigation,” a TV series that presents dramatized reconstructions of real air disasters.

On Thursday, Israeli President Isaac Herzog announced he was nominating Hayoun and three other passengers involved in the intervention effort for the Presidential Award ​for Civilian Heroism. 

“Everyone who was there in those moments, the passengers and the crew, mobilized, acted with courage, supported one another in mutual responsibility, and helped prevent a severe disaster,” Herzog wrote in a social media post translated from Hebrew.

The flight, which was en route to Tel Aviv, was diverted for an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia after a second air crew aboard the plane took over the controls. 

Indian Airline Capt. Smit Machchhar was taken to the hospital for treatment to receive medical attention for stab wounds he sustained during the attack. His co-pilot was arrested and interrogated by Saudi authorities, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Wednesday. 

Trump noted in his Friday video message that Hayoun was “a Trump fan,” referencing the plumber’s message of support for the U.S. president during a conversation with Netanyahu after the incident.

“I’m a fan of his. A big fan,” Trump said in the clip.

data.title: SCOTUS must show oil companies they aren't above local accountability
data.description:
A basic moral principle is also a rule of law: If you lie about something and your lies cause harm, you should compensate people you injured. Sounds simple, but what counts as harm, whether the lie caused it, and what compensation is appropriate can be hard questions. Judges and juries wrestle with them every day. 

On the first day of its new term, the Supreme Court will hear a bold argument: that no jury can even consider these questions when the allegations concern deception by fossil fuel companies about climate change. In Suncor v. Boulder County, two oil companies will be making that case to stop a lawsuit against them. If you think people should be able to hold corporations accountable in court, you should pay attention.   

For decades, oil companies have cast doubt on climate change and the idea that burning fossil fuels might be to blame. But about a decade ago, investigators uncovered a trove of documents showing the industry knew the truth since at least the 1960s.    

Specifically, oil and gas executives knew their industry and products were releasing huge amounts of carbon dioxide, which was causing the atmosphere to heat to a point that it could lead to — in their words — “globally catastrophic events” by the end of this century. They knew the only “uncertainty” in this chain of events was whether they would disclose the problem or do anything to reduce the level of carbon dioxide entering the atmosphere.  

States and local governments struggling with expensive and avoidable climate-related damage took notice. Dozens — including Boulder County — sued oil companies under state consumer protection and product safety laws, alleging decades of industry deception.   

It’s hardly the first time that local governments have sued an industry for hurting people by hiding the truth. A generation ago, thousands successfully sued tobacco companies to recover the costs of caring for smokers who were told cigarettes were safe. More recently, all 50 states did the same to companies who hid the truth about opioids.    

The fossil fuel industry desperately wants to avoid that fate. Big Oil companies are trying to stop these lawsuits — not by contesting the claims but blocking state courts from hearing them.   

To be clear, the state and local government lawsuits aren’t trying to regulate things like oil wells, air pollution or the car you drive. Those topics are generally covered by federal laws and contested in federal courts. The lawsuits aim to make the oil companies that lied about the risks of their products help pay for the damages those products caused. That’s the kind of case that state courts handle all the time.  

Maybe you agree with the oil companies that it’s not fair to blame them for global climate change. Maybe you think that they didn’t really deceive anyone, or that the deception didn’t cause climate change or that climate change isn’t really causing damage. But this Supreme Court case is just about whether a jury should have the chance to consider those questions.  

The oil companies’ most radical argument is that abstract constitutional principles shield them from being sued in state court for deceiving people. That boils down to a policy argument that the oil industry is just too important to have to answer to local governments that are dealing with the costs of climate-related damage.

Courts are meant to rule on questions of law, not policy. So, I wasn’t surprised when the Colorado Supreme Court rejected the industry’s arguments, paving the way for an actual trial. I also wasn’t surprised when the oil companies asked the Supreme Court to review that decision. No harm in trying.

But I was surprised when the court agreed to get involved before the plaintiffs even got their day in court; it had declined to get involved in similar cases on five recent occasions. Perhaps the conservative majority is itching, as many suspect, to continue its streak of prioritizing corporations over people’s health and the environment.  

And I was even more surprised at the latest plot twist: Justice Alito recused himself from Suncor just one week before oral arguments. The justice didn’t explain why he bowed out, but people had been calling on him to do so because he has financial investments in the oil industry. That leaves the remaining justices to answer questions they may never have wanted to take up. At least four justices have to vote to take up a case; we don’t know if Justice Alito provided one of them.

But even without Alito, we should all still ask the same question: If the Supreme Court gives Big Oil a hall pass, which industry will be clamoring to be next? AI companies? Pharmaceutical giants?  

I hope the court does the right thing and lets this case proceed. It’s hardly the court’s last chance to consider these questions. It can always take the case up after the plaintiffs get their day in court, and after a jury has made its findings.

The rule of law works best when it’s applied to everyone equally. This case will be a good test of whether the Justices believe that.

Sambhav Sankar is senior vice president for programs at Earthjustice.

data.title: Deadline to reduce your student loan interest rate extended: What to know
data.description:
(NEXSTAR) – A day before the deadline was set to end, the Education Department extended the window in which student loan borrowers can get a small reduction on their interest rates.

Earlier this summer, the Education Department announced that borrowers could get a 1% decrease on their interest rates through the end of June 2028. At the time, borrowers had until Sept. 30 of this year to apply.

On Tuesday, just before that deadline, the Education Department said it would extend the application deadline.

Here’s what to know.

How to get the 1% interest rate reduction

It’s relatively simple. You need to enroll in auto pay on your student loans by the new deadline, which is Dec. 31, 2026.

Earlier this year, the Education Department said only about 40% of borrowers were paying their loans via auto pay. Nearly 2 million more enrolled after the 1% reduction was announced.

If you are already enrolled in auto pay, you should be receiving that reduction. Prior to July 1 of this year, you would receive a 0.25% reduction to your interest rate for auto pay enrollment.

If you are not yet enrolled, you’ll need to access your loan servicer account. There, you should find an option to enter your bank account information and specify payment amounts to set up auto pay.

If you are in default on your federal student loans, the Education Department says you will need to consolidate your eligible loans via StudentAid.gov and apply for a new repayment plan before being eligible for auto pay.

Once on auto pay, the department said you will need to remain there and “meet all eligibility criteria” to continue receiving the 1% interest rate reduction. That includes having loans that “originate after July 1, 2012.”

Auto pay has other benefits, Education Department says

In addition to the interest rate deduction, being enrolled in auto pay grants “access to key benefits,” officials said.

They pointed to the Repayment Assistance Plan, a recently released repayment option that gives borrowers “a match on their on-time payments to ensure interest does not accrue and balances decline every month.”

On-time payments are also crucial to borrowers pursuing Public Service Loan Forgiveness, the Education Department explained.

Other changes may have impacted your loans this summer

In addition to the higher interest rate deduction rolled out this summer, the Education Department enacted other changes that may have impacted how you borrow or pay back federal loans.

Potentially the largest change was the end of the Biden-era Saving on a Valuable Education plan (better known as the SAVE plan), which gave some of its 7 million federal student loan borrowers monthly payments as low as $0. Impacted borrowers were set to be notified in July that they would need to switch to a different repayment plan.

Limits on Parent PLUS loans and repayment options also took effect this summer, as did limits on how much graduate students can borrow. All borrowers, for the first time, have a lifetime limit on how much they can borrow in federal student loans.
